processing: Bred for kamairi tamaryokucha, a pan-fired green tea rolled into curled shapes; today it also goes into lightly withered sencha, oolong and Japanese black tea.
harvest_season: Normal budding for a Japanese cultivar, so green tea lots are typically spring pickings; black tea makers may pick later in the year as well.
appearance_dry: As a pan-fired green, curled dark green leaf of good shape; as a black tea, dark twisted leaf, typical of Japanese black teas.
appearance_liquor: Yellow-green and clear as a pan-fired green tea, coppery as a black tea, as is typical of those styles.
appearance_wet: Medium green opened leaf in the green style, coppery brown in the black style, as is usual for each.
taste_profile: As a pan-fired green it is full-bodied and intense, with an aroma unusual among Japanese cultivars. As a black tea it runs light, fruity and mineral.

brewing.notes: A starting point for the green style, typical of pan-fired Japanese greens. For black Izumi use water near boiling and about three minutes.

vintage_note: A rare single-cultivar tea from a handful of farmers, sold in small lots by harvest year. Green and oolong versions are best within a year or so of picking, and black tea keeps somewhat longer. The label should state the style, because the same cultivar can reach you as any of several very different teas.
description:
Izumi is an old and rare Japanese cultivar with an unusual purpose: it was bred to make pan-fired green tea for export to North Africa, where Japanese growers wanted to compete with Chinese green tea. Only a few farmers grow it now.

The plant is vigorous, cold-hardy and heavy-yielding, though very prone to net blister blight, which helps explain why it is not widely planted. It descends from seed collected in a Benihomare field, and Benihomare is a black tea cultivar, so it is not surprising that the leaf also suits oxidised styles.

In the cup, the pan-fired version is praised for intense flavour and a distinctive aroma. Black tea versions come across as lighter, with a mineral and fruity character. Treat the brewing numbers as style-specific, since a green Izumi steeped like a black one will turn harsh.

Expect to buy it from small Kyushu gardens as a single-cultivar lot, with the style and harvest year named. If you like Japanese black tea, it makes an interesting comparison with Benihomare itself.
history:
In 1933 seed was collected from a Benihomare field at the Fukuoka prefectural agricultural experiment station and sown elsewhere; the best seedling was selected, and the cultivar was registered in 1960 through the Kyushu agricultural experiment station.

It stayed a rare cultivar. Interest returned in 2008, when a lightly withered sencha and an oolong made from Izumi won top prizes at the World Green Tea Contest, and it has since drawn attention from makers of Japanese black tea.
